[0] Court filings have contradicted earlier suggestions that a former Apple employee could retain access to confidential files after leaving the company to join OpenAI.

[1] There was speculation that the file access may have simply been an accident, with Apple's iCloud arrangements seemingly in disarray – but Apple says that wasn't the case…

[2] Quick recap

[3] Apple sued OpenAI last month, accusing the company of stealing trade secrets related to a hardware project. One of the allegations focused on a former Apple employee named Chang Liu, who subsequently joined OpenAI. The rough timeline of events is as follows:

  • [4] July 10: Apple files lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that a former Apple employee systematically stole Apple's trade secrets to benefit the OpenAI hardware team they subsequently joined
  • [5] July 10: OpenAI issues a brief denial statement
  • [6] July 14: OpenAI updates its response, saying it has seen no evidence to support Apple's allegations
  • [7] August 3: OpenAI publishes a blog post attacking Apple's lawsuit
  • [8] August 4: Apple applies for a temporary restraining order to prevent "irreparable harm"

[9] The iCloud mess

[10] OpenAI said that an information security loophole within Apple resulted in the former employee retaining "unnecessary" access to confidential files after leaving.

[11] Earlier, The Information published a report identifying this as the iCloud arrangement disarray OpenAI was referring to.

[12] The report said that, while Apple revokes former employees' access to company-managed iCloud folders, it appears that many files may have been shared to the employee's personal account – which not only retained access after they left, but could even receive push updates.

[13] In other words, the former employee's personal devices could automatically receive updates to confidential files, without the individual doing anything wrong.

[14] Apple says that's not the case

[15] However, John Gruber of Daring Fireball pointed out that Apple stated in their court filings that those files were not stored on iCloud.

[16] Gruber believes the files were almost certainly stored on Box, a cloud storage service widely used within Apple.

[17] 9to5Mac's take

[18] For now, both sides' accounts remain at odds, and we'll have to wait until the case goes to trial to sort out what's true and what isn't.

[19] However, Apple does appear to have tacitly acknowledged the existence of an iCloud mess. The arrangement is reportedly intended to prevent Apple employees from having to carry both work and personal iPhones. While understandable, the setup does appear to create an obvious security hole.
